title: A clean kitchen, safe drinking water and a home pests cannot use

say: A clean kitchen, safe drinking water and a home pests cannot use.
This is the video for module 2 of Home Hygiene and Sanitation: Kitchen, Water and Pest Control.
Most kitchen illness does not come from dramatic mistakes. It comes from small habits, like the same wet cloth used on the table, the plates and the baby's face.

say: Keep raw food and ready food apart. Use two boards, one marked for raw meat, or cut ready foods first and wash the board. Give cloths separate jobs, and dry them in the sun every day.

say: Clear water from a well, tanker or roadside seller can still carry cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea germs.

say: If it is cloudy, let it stand covered for several hours, then pour off the clearer water.

say: Filter it through a clean cloth folded several times. But cloth alone does not make water safe.

say: Then bring it to a rolling boil, where big bubbles keep coming even when you stir.
WHO says this is enough to inactivate disease-causing germs.
Or use chlorine tablets or liquid exactly as the label says.
Turn pot handles inward, away from children.

say: For example, Ngozi in Onitsha buys tanker water and is not sure of its source, so she boils all drinking water. She measures for three days and plans for 12 litres a day.

panel.heading: Ngozi plans a day's safe water
items: Family of five: about 12 litres a day
4-litre pot: 12 / 4 = 3 boils a day
Two 10-litre containers with taps
One in use, one filling and cooling
Washed every Saturday, labelled

say: Her pot holds 4 litres, so she needs 3 boils: one in the morning and two in the evening, when the stove is already on.

say: WHO links Lassa fever to the Mastomys rat.
People are infected mainly through food or household items touched by rat urine or faeces.
So store grain and dry foods in containers with tight lids, not open sacks, and bring drying food in before dark.

cards.d: Grain, garri and rice in containers with tight lids. Never dry food on bare ground overnight.
Bin with a lid, rubbish far from home. Close gaps and holes with cement or wire mesh.
Gloves on. Wet droppings with soapy water or disinfectant first. Never sweep them dry.

say: Keep rubbish in a lidded bin and dispose of it far from the home. Close holes in walls, gaps under doors and open drains.

say: Never sweep droppings dry, because it raises dust. Wear gloves, wet them first, wait a few minutes, wipe up, and throw away any food rats have touched.

say: For example, Funke in Ondo hears rats at night.
She finds 3 holes in the walls, an open drain, and a gap under the door.
Her garri, rice and beans are in open sacks.
She buys 3 buckets with tight lids at about 3,500 naira each.
For repairs: cement for the holes, wire mesh for the drain, and a door sweep.
About 20,500 naira in total. These prices are approximate. She removes the rats' food and their way in, and checks again after two weeks for fresh droppings.
To remember.
Keep raw and ready food apart.
Wash and rinse in two basins.
Boil or treat water and store it covered.
Keep food in rodent-proof containers.
And empty anything holding water each week, so mosquitoes cannot breed.
Use poisons last, locked away from children.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Raw and ready food apart; cloths with one job
Wash, rinse, dry off the floor
Settle, filter, boil; store covered with a tap
Rodent-proof food stores; rubbish far away
Empty standing water weekly for mosquitoes
